# Litigation

We can take a matter to court where there has been a contravention of Australian workplace laws. For example, if an employer refuses to pay their employees what they’re owed.

## On this page:

- [When we take a matter to court](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/compliance-and-enforcement/litigation#when-we-take-a-matter-to-court)
- [Court orders](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/compliance-and-enforcement/litigation#court-orders)
- [Serious contravention](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/compliance-and-enforcement/litigation#serious-contraventions)
- [When there are no records](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/compliance-and-enforcement/litigation#when-there-are-no-records)
- [Tools and resources](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/compliance-and-enforcement/litigation#tools-and-resources)
- [Related information](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/compliance-and-enforcement/litigation#related-information)

## When we take a matter to court

Our decision to take a matter to court (also known as initiating civil litigation) will depend on whether we have enough evidence and whether it’s in the public interest. Our [Compliance and Enforcement Policy](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/sites/default/files/migration/725/compliance-and-enforcement-policy.docx "Compliance and enforcement policy [DOCX]") [Compliance and Enforcement Policy](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/sites/default/files/migration/725/compliance-and-enforcement-policy.pdf "Compliance and enforcement policy [PDF]") talks about these factors in more detail.

If the employer is a company, we can take the company to court, but we can also take a person to court if they were involved in the company’s contravention. A person involved in the company’s contravention can include:

- a company director
- a human resources manager or other manager
- an accountant
- a business involved in the [supply chain](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/find-help-for/labour-hire-and-supply-chains "Labour hire and supply chains").

If you’re thinking about taking your own legal action and your claim is for an amount of $100,000 or less, find out more at [Small claims court](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/workplace-problems/fixing-a-workplace-problem/other-workplace-relations-help/small-claims-court "Small claims court").

### Criminal offences

From 1 January 2025, intentionally underpaying an employee can be a criminal offence. Honest mistakes aren’t considered a criminal offence.

We can investigate suspected criminal underpayment offences and refer matters to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions or the Australian Federal Police for possible criminal prosecution.

For more information, go to [Criminal prosecution](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/compliance-and-enforcement/criminal-prosecution "Criminal prosecution").

## Court orders

If civil litigation is successful, a court may impose orders against a person found to have done the wrong thing. Those court orders may:

- make a person pay an amount of money as a [penalty](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/compliance-and-enforcement/litigation#civil-penalty-amounts) for not doing what the law says
- make an employer who has been issued with a notice (for example, a compliance notice or a notice to produce records) comply, wholly or partly, with its terms
- make an employer or other person pay an employee their outstanding entitlements (plus interest)
- require someone to do something (for example, give an employee their job back) or undertake training or do an audit
- restrain someone from doing something (an injunction or interim injunction) for example, stop discriminating against an employee
- pay an employee compensation for loss suffered.

### Civil penalty amounts

Only a court can determine a penalty amount to be paid. Civil penalty amounts can be up to:

- for an individual:
  - $21,840 per contravention
  - $218,400 per contravention for some 'serious contraventions'
- for a company with less than 15 employees:
  - $109,200 per contravention
  - $1,092,000 per contravention for some 'serious contraventions'
- for a company with 15 or more employees:
  - $546,000, or for contraventions relating to an underpayment, the greater of $546,000 or 3 times the underpayment amount per contravention.
  - $5,460,000 per contravention for some 'serious contraventions'.

## Serious contraventions

A serious contravention happens when the court finds that:

- the person or business knew they were contravening an obligation under workplace laws, or
- the person or business was reckless as to whether the contravention would occur.

The higher penalties for serious contraventions apply to breaches of:

- the [National Employment Standards](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/employment-conditions/national-employment-standards "National Employment Standards")
- a [modern award](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/node/327 "Awards Archived")
- an [enterprise agreement](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/employment-conditions/agreements "Agreements")
- a [workplace determination](https://www.fwc.gov.au/workplace-determinations)
- a [national minimum wage order](https://www.fwc.gov.au/work-conditions/minimum-wages-and-conditions/national-minimum-wage/national-minimum-wage-orders)
- an [equal remuneration wage order](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/tools-and-resources/best-practice-guides/gender-pay-equity "Gender pay equity best practice guide")
- [method and frequency of paying wages](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/pay-and-wages/paying-wages/frequency-of-pay "Frequency of pay")
- [unlawful deductions including cashback schemes](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/pay-and-wages/deductions-and-related-issues "Deductions and related issues")
- [guarantees of annual earnings](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/awards-and-agreements/award-and-agreement-free-wages-and-conditions#employee-award-free)
- [record-keeping requirements](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/pay-and-wages/paying-wages/record-keeping "Record-keeping"), and
- [pay slip requirements](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/pay-and-wages/paying-wages/pay-slips "Pay slips").

If someone else was involved in the contravention, and knew it was a contravention, they could also face higher penalties.

## When there are no records

If an employer doesn't meet their record-keeping or pay slip obligations, and can't give a reasonable excuse, they will need to disprove allegations in wage claims made in a court. This is sometimes referred to as a 'reverse onus of proof.'

This applies in court proceedings relating to breaches of:

- the [National Employment Standards](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/employment-conditions/national-employment-standards "National Employment Standards")
- a [modern award](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/node/327 "Awards Archived")
- an [enterprise agreement](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/employment-conditions/agreements "Agreements")
- a [workplace determination](https://www.fwc.gov.au/workplace-determinations)
- a [national minimum wage order](https://www.fwc.gov.au/work-conditions/minimum-wages-and-conditions/national-minimum-wage/national-minimum-wage-orders)
- an [equal remuneration wage order](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/tools-and-resources/best-practice-guides/gender-pay-equity "Gender pay equity best practice guide")
- [unlawful deductions including cashback schemes](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/pay-and-wages/deductions-and-related-issues "Deductions and related issues")
- [method and frequency of paying wages](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/pay-and-wages/paying-wages/frequency-of-pay "Frequency of pay").

If an employee makes a claim for breach of one or more of the above obligations and the employer didn’t keep the right records, make those records available, or give them a pay slip, the employer needs to prove that they did pay the employee correctly or gave them the right entitlements.

Check [Pay slip and record-keeping obligations](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/pay-and-wages/paying-wages/payment-summaries-and-income-statements "Payment summaries and income statements") for information about what records employers need to keep.

Source reference for page: [Fair Work Act 2009 sections 537–547, 557–557C](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2009A00028/latest/text)
